data.title: Pound Has Chances To Close The Week With Moderate Gains
data.description:
GBP/USD is trading at 1.31026 on Friday. Despite attempts to recover during the week, the British currency continues to experience pressure from the dollar. Trading activity may remain subdued today due to the shortened post-Thanksgiving US session.

The main factor supporting the dollar remains the outlook for Fed monetary policy. PCE and third-quarter US GDP data published on Wednesday confirmed the stability of the American economy in the presence of high inflation. In addition to the expected 25 basis point rate hike in December, markets are pricing in two more increases in early 2027.

The geopolitical situation also contributes to sustained demand for the American currency. Recent statements by Donald Trump have provided no clarity on the prospects for an agreement with Iran, while the intensification of confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthis expands risks to the region's energy infrastructure.

At the same time, the potential for a further decline in the pound is limited by expectations of Bank of England policy tightening. Investors are increasingly pricing in a rate increase in December and expect this process to continue in 2027.

In the absence of significant macroeconomic data from the UK and the US, GBP/USD dynamics today will be determined mainly by geopolitical news and market sentiment. Despite current pressure, the pound has a chance to close the week with moderate gains for the first time in four weeks.

Technical Analysis

On the four-hour GBP/USD chart, the market continues to develop a downward wave with the main estimated target at 1.2620. Following the local minimum, an upward correction has formed. Today, the corrective movement is expected to continue towards the 1.3141 level. After its development, the likelihood of a resumption of the decline towards 1.3010 will be considered. A breakdown of this level would open the prospect of a continuation of the downward wave towards 1.2855. This mark is considered a local target and corresponds to the intermediate stage of the main descending structure. The ultimate goal of the current wave remains 1.2620. Technically, the MACD indicator confirms the possibility of the correction continuing. Its signal line is approaching zero from below and pointing upwards. The reduction in the histogram's negative values indicates a weakening of downward momentum, though the main trend continues.

On the hourly GBP/USD chart, the market has formed a consolidation range around the 1.3074 level. The price has now found support at 1.3094 and continues to develop the upward leg of the correction. Today, a rise towards 1.3142 with resistance tested from below is expected. After the correction is completed, a resumption of movement along the main trend towards the 1.3010 target will be considered. Technically, the possibility of short-term growth is supported by the Stochastic oscillator. Its signal lines are above the 50 level, near the 70 mark, with potential for a further move towards 80. A subsequent downward turn in the oscillator may provide further confirmation that the upward correction is complete. The priority scenario remains a resumption of the downward movement after testing the nearest resistance.

Conclusion

GBP/USD is trading around 1.31026, with the pound attempting to recover despite continued dollar strength. The dollar remains supported by hawkish Fed expectations, with a December hike fully priced and two more increases anticipated in early 2027, alongside stable US economic data and geopolitical uncertainty. However, the pound's downside is limited by growing expectations of a BoE rate hike in December and further tightening in 2027. With no major UK or US data due today and a shortened US session, geopolitical news and market sentiment will drive the pair. Technically, the broader downtrend remains intact, with the main target at 1.2620, but a corrective move towards 1.3141 is expected before the decline resumes towards 1.3010 and potentially 1.2855. The pound has a chance to close the week with moderate gains for the first time in four weeks, though the overall structure remains bearish.

data.title: Rates Spark: Rates Resist Bearish Pressure As France Faces Rating Risk
data.description:
Bearish dynamics remain contained in European rates despite the ECB’s tightening bias and firmer energy prices. French spreads tightened ahead of S&P’s review, but political uncertainty and budget risks could warrant a negative outlook – and keep investors cautious

Bearish dynamics remain contained

Left on their own with the US out on holiday, European rates briefly tested the upside. While the European Central Bank accounts clearly pointed to the ECB’s tightening bias – maybe even beyond December – and energy prices also sneaked higher as tensions in the Middle East continue to simmer, a bearish dynamic failed to take hold in the end. What lingers is the uncertainty around the tech narrative.

S&P scheduled to review France after Friday’s market close

French bond spreads did manage to tighten over the past session, taking the 10y spread over Bunds below the 150bp threshold.

This seems to defy the risk of S&P lowering the outlook on the stable A+ rating it currently still attaches to France. Given the uncertain political backdrop, further budget slippage over the year and an eroding growth outlook, S&P may have enough reason to do just that. At the same time, it would no longer really come as a surprise. Fitch lowered the outlook of its A+ rating to negative at the end of October in an unscheduled move after having only just reviewed the country in August.

Moreover, markets are already pricing France more like a BBB-rated country. To be fair, much of this is likely an overshoot. In its recent Financial Stability Review, the ECB pointed to the procyclical role of hedge funds in eurozone government bond spread dynamics. At the same time, the lingering threat of a downgrade might create another hurdle for investors looking to return to the French bond market.

Replacing hedge fund demand may come at a costs to gilts

The Bank of England has reiterated its intention to introduce measures to strengthen the gilt repo market, which could negatively impact demand for gilts. Hedge funds have acted as an important marginal buyer over the past year, helping absorb the significant increase in gilt supply. A popular strategy is buying cash gilts and offsetting these positions with shorts in gilt futures, whereby repo markets offer the ability to leverage up such trades. The slight pricing difference between cash gilts and gilt futures can provide attractive returns. But if the repo costs were to rise, the attractiveness of such trades could fall.

In effect, hedge funds offer balance sheet capacity to house gilts, and therefore any headwinds to such trades can add upward pressure to gilt yields. But the impact is more nuanced. Because the gilt positions are hedged through futures, any unwind of the hedge fund positions should be relatively neutral in terms of term premium. We would, however, expect gilts to underperform swaps. The spread between swaps and gilts is strongly linked to the balance sheet costs of holding bonds. If hedge funds decide a trade is no longer attractive due to higher trading costs, then other players with higher balance sheet costs (such as banks) would have to jump in.

Friday's events and market view

We will see preliminary inflation data for November in France and Spain, where headline rates are expected to ease somewhat but remain at elevated levels. The ECB will also publish its consumer survey on expected inflation. ECB officials scheduled to speak are Chief Economist Philip Lane, Vice President Boris Vujčić, Germany's Joachim Nagel and France's Emmanuel Moulin.

In primary markets, Italy will auction 5y and 10y BTPS as well as 8y and 9y CCTeu floaters (in total up to 8bn).

data.title: United States Dollar Index Weakens Below 104.00 As AI Concerns Simmer
data.description:
The US Dollar Index (DXY), an index of the value of the US Dollar (USD) measured against a basket of six world currencies, currently trades near 103.70 in the early European trading hours on Friday. The DXY declines as traders look to equity markets for clues on direction as doubts about the AI trade trigger heightened volatility.

The DXY remains choppy, as markets are concerned that a deeper AI slowdown could weigh on US growth. However, the potential downside for the index might be limited amid expectations for US Federal Reserve (Fed) policy tightening.

"All eyes are on whether the downtrend in AI-related stocks will turn around," said Mizuho analysts.

Hotter-than-expected US core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation in October, continued economic growth, and hawkish comments from Fed officials lift the USD against its rivals.

The Fed’s preferred gauge of inflation, the US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, jumped 3.8% in October from the previous year, the US Bureau of Economic Analysis showed on Wednesday. Excluding food and energy, so-called core PCE rose 3.3% YoY in October, above the market consensus of 3.2%. 

Fed Governor Christopher Waller signaled that he could support a larger half-percentage-point move to curb inflation. Traders are now seeing a quarter-point interest rate hike on December 9 as a near certainty, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.

"The risk-reward of chasing further USD gains looks less attractive, but hawkish Fed risks should keep the dollar supported," said Sim Moh Siong, an FX strategist at OCBC in Singapore.

Dollar gains as tighter US financial conditions temper Fed hike path

Analysts at MUFG/BTMU highlight that the US Dollar "has continued to strengthen amidst the deepening sell-off in US stocks and pullback for US yields from year-to-date highs." They note that the latest bout of "weakness in the US equity market is taking place at a time when there is building evidence of strengthening cyclical growth momentum in the US," a combination that is "encouraging a stronger US dollar."

In MUFG/BTMU’s view, this "strengthening cyclical momentum is encouraging the Fed to raise rates further into restrictive territory in an attempt to dampen growth and ease upside inflation risks." At the same time, they caution that "the Fed will also be wary of the risk that a more sustained period of equity market weakness and tightening of financial conditions, including a stronger US dollar, would help to dampen the need for rate hikes."

MUFG/BTMU point out that "financial conditions have tightened sharply since the Fed indicated it is considering speeding up the pace of rate hikes in the coming months," a shift that "partly reflect[s] fears that the Fed could overtighten policy." This balance between robust cyclical momentum and rapidly tightening financial conditions is seen as central to the Dollar’s current support and to the Fed’s evolving policy calculus.

Williams flags more Fed work on inflation, keeping Dollar bulls alert

Fed’s Williams delivers a speech that is broadly consistent with the established baseline, with the FXS Speechtracker score holding at 6.2/10, exactly in line with the historical average. The emphasis that the U.S. central bank “still has work to do” to get inflation back to the 2% target, alongside projections of 3.5% inflation in 2026 and a return to 2% only by 2028, underscores a still-hawkish bias despite acknowledging stable jobs and a resilient economy. While Williams notes that inflation pressures are not broadening much, the characterization of inflation as “still too high” with upside risks keeps the policy narrative tilted toward further restraint rather than imminent easing, a backdrop that tends to support the Dollar on balance.

The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rose by 0.35 points to 152.49, reinforcing that the overall policy tone remains firmly in hawkish territory well above the neutral 100 threshold. This incremental uptick, aligned with the steady 6.2/10 FXS Speechtracker score, signals that markets should continue to price a relatively restrictive Fed stance, with limited scope for near-term dovish surprises.

Technical Analysis: US Dollar Index retains a positive view in the near term

In the daily chart, Dollar Index Spot trades at 103.70. The near-term bias is bullish as price holds above the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) at 101.09 and the Bollinger Bands’ middle band at roughly 103.03, reinforcing an underlying bid after the recent breakout. The Relative Strength Index (14) at 61.36 stays in positive territory without being overbought, suggesting constructive momentum that could keep the index supported on dips.

On the downside, initial support is seen at the Bollinger middle band near 103.03, ahead of a broader demand zone defined by the lower Bollinger band at around 101.19 and the 100-day SMA at 101.09. On the topside, the Bollinger upper band at 104.87 acts as the next resistance, and a sustained move above this barrier would open the way for an extension of the current advance.

data.title: Week Ahead: US Jobs Take Centre Stage
data.description:
Five days. Three labor market reports. One crucial test for the dollar.

The US labor market will dominate the first week of December as investors assess whether employment remains strong enough to keep the Federal Reserve cautious about interest rates.

Tuesday's JOLTS report and Wednesday's ADP employment figures will set the stage for Friday's Non-Farm Payrolls release.

And the stakes are high.

The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, while unemployment stood at 4.1%. Average hourly earnings increased by 0.4% month-on-month, highlighting continued wage pressures.

Stronger employment figures could reinforce expectations that the Fed will maintain restrictive monetary policy, supporting the dollar and potentially weighing on gold. Softer data may revive expectations of future rate cuts.

Our focus this week will be on Alpari's EURUSD and Gold (XAUUSD), with both instruments potentially facing increased volatility as markets reassess the outlook for US interest rates.

US labor market in focus

Investors will closely monitor US employment data, business activity and Eurozone inflation as markets assess the outlook for global growth and monetary policy. Friday's Non-Farm Payrolls report could become the week's main volatility trigger.

Tuesday, December 1st: Eurozone CPI and US JOLTS

Eurozone annual inflation previously stood at 4.0%, while US job openings reached 7.523 million in September. The reports could influence expectations around ECB policy and provide early clues on US labor demand.

Wednesday, December 2nd: US ADP Employment

Private-sector employment increased by 86,000 in October. November's ADP report will offer another indication of hiring trends ahead of Friday's official labor market figures.

Thursday, December 3rd: US ISM Services PMI

The services PMI previously stood at 54.5, indicating continued expansion. The November reading could provide fresh insight into economic momentum and underlying price pressures.

Friday, December 4th: US Non-Farm Payrolls

The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October, with unemployment at 4.1% and monthly wage growth at 0.4%. November's report could reshape expectations around the Fed's next policy decisions and trigger sharp moves in the dollar and gold.

data.title: Oil: The Market Has Already Written Off The Energy Crisis
data.description:
As investors turn their attention back to technology stocks, the market seems to believe that the oil crisis is now behind us. The spectacular drop in prices since October has helped reassure financial markets, which are anticipating a normalization of supply conditions and a retreat in inflationary pressures.

This complacency is dangerous. Behind the decline in paper oil prices, the fundamentals of the physical market continue to deteriorate. Inventories are falling, flows through the Strait of Hormuz are contracting again, and the structure of futures contracts points to mounting pressure on near-term supply.

From a technical perspective, WTI crude has been trading within a broad contracting triangle since March. The recent correction has formed a bullish harmonic pattern known as a Bullish Bat, whose completion point D coincides with the triangle’s lower boundary, around $80. Although the Fibonacci ratios do not perfectly match those of a textbook pattern, this convergence of technical support levels strengthens the likelihood of a rebound. The chart target for this move lies at the triangle’s upper boundary, in a zone between $98 and $102 per barrel. This bullish scenario remains valid as long as the ascending trendline support holds.

Inventories falling out of season

At this time of year, crude oil inventories normally tend to build as demand slows seasonally.

Yet the latest US statistics paint a very different picture. Total petroleum stocks fell by 5.3 million barrels in one week, despite another 2.9 million-barrel drawdown from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR):

Commercial crude inventories did increase by 1.1 million barrels, but total commercial stocks of petroleum and refined products fell by 2.4 million barrels.

US strategic reserves now contain just 273.5 million barrels.

The oil surplus that financial markets regularly talk about fails to materialize in the inventory data.

Hormuz: flows deteriorate again

The situation in the Strait of Hormuz is deteriorating once more.

Oil flows through the strait have fallen back to around 6 million barrels per day on a seven-day average, compared with 20 million before the conflict:

More concerning still, a substantial gap is emerging between volumes loaded inside the Persian Gulf and those that actually make it through the strait.

Oil loadings in the Persian Gulf are running at nearly 16 million barrels per day, yet only 6 million barrels are currently passing through the Strait of Hormuz.

This gap suggests that oil is accumulating inside the Gulf, although the latest shipping data are preliminary and transit times need to be taken into account.

The market now appears convinced that Iran lacks both the means and the willingness to escalate the conflict. The absence of escalation around the Fujairah and Sohar transshipment hubs reinforces this view among traders.

But no one really knows Iran’s strategy – or its timeline.

The current status quo appears difficult to sustain. Any further escalation before year-end would come as political pressure on Donald Trump intensifies and oil reserve levels constrain the US room for maneuver.

The futures market is sending a warning signal

While oil prices have undergone a sharp correction, the spread between the first two Brent futures contracts has surged back to $3.82:

In practical terms, oil for delivery in January 2027 is trading $3.82 higher than oil for delivery in February.

This structure, known as backwardation, reflects a premium for immediate access to oil.

In a genuinely oversupplied market, one would expect the opposite. Traders would be incentivized to store oil and sell it later at a higher price.

Today, the market is instead rewarding prompt availability of barrels.

The spectacular decline in paper oil prices therefore masks persistent tightness in the front end of the curve.

Falling oil prices will not rescue the Fed

The compression of paper oil prices has an obvious political benefit: lowering inflation expectations and reassuring bond markets.

But the latest US inflation figures show the limits of this strategy.

The PCE index, the inflation gauge preferred by the Federal Reserve, continues to climb:

In October, US inflation measured by the PCE index reached 3.8% year-on-year, while core inflation, excluding energy and food, stood at 3.3% – well above the Fed’s 2% target.

Despite easing energy prices, underlying inflationary pressures are intensifying. US third-quarter growth has also just been revised up to 4.3% annualized.

Under these circumstances, the Fed is likely to raise rates in December. Markets are also anticipating another hike in January.

What happens if oil prices rise again while the Fed is already being forced to tighten monetary policy?

It’s not 2020 – but possibly 2022

Investors still seem to be thinking in terms of the 2020 scenario, when the collapse in financial markets triggered a historic drop in oil demand.

The current situation is radically different.

The main risk is not a collapse in demand, but a contraction in supply. In this respect, the comparison with 2022 seems far more relevant: equity markets can suffer sharp corrections while energy prices continue to rise.

Oil could therefore decouple from other financial assets during the next waves of equity-market liquidation.

If flows through Hormuz do not recover quickly, current prices could represent one of the last opportunities to buy a barrel below $100. In a scenario of prolonged shortages, that level could even become a floor in 2027.

The market has stopped paying attention to oil precisely when it should be watching it most closely.

The combination of another energy shock, persistent inflation and rising rates is likely to be one of the most underestimated risks facing financial markets as 2027 approaches.

Gold and the risk of another inflation shock

In the short term, the prospect of further Fed tightening and liquidity pressures could continue to weigh on gold prices. Over the medium term, however, another oil shock would confront central banks with a formidable dilemma: fighting inflation at the risk of triggering a financial crisis amid widespread excessive debt. Unlike in 2022, governments now have even less fiscal room to maneuver. Higher interest rates would substantially increase debt-servicing costs, while rising energy prices would undermine the real economy. It is precisely this monetary and fiscal predicament that reinforces gold’s appeal as a long-term protective asset.

data.title: Gold Declines To Near $3,550 Amid Hawkish Fed Expectations
data.description:
Gold price edges lower to around $3,565 during the early Asian session on Friday. The precious metal faces some selling pressure amid inflation concerns and expectations of a US Federal Reserve (Fed) interest rate hike next month. The price fell to its lowest level since August 2025 in the previous session, as the US Thanksgiving holiday kept trading volumes subdued.

On Wednesday, the release of the US October Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, the Fed’s preferred measure of underlying inflation, reinforced expectations that the US central bank will tighten policy next month and again in early 2027. Higher borrowing costs are a headwind for gold as it doesn’t pay interest.

"Spot gold is testing support around the mid-$3,000 region. Gold is unlikely to see a sustained rebound until markets sense that the Fed is nearing the end of its rate-hike cycle," said Han Tan, chief market analyst at Bybit. "Bullion bulls are set to be kept on the back foot... But fresh risk-off events across global financial markets may support the precious metal, adding to persistent purchases from central banks,” Han added.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump prepared to raise tariffs on China, the European Union (EU), Mexico, Japan and dozens of other countries that Trump argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, per the Wall Street Journal. Any signs of renewed trade tensions could boost safe-haven flows, benefiting the yellow metal in the near term.

Precious metals whipsaw as copper grinds to new lows

Analysts at Deutsche Bank highlight that “another asset class that saw some big moves over the last 24 hours were precious metals,” with price action turning notably volatile. They point out that Gold “fell as much as -3.66% intra-day, which put it on course for its lowest level since August 2025, but it recovered to +0.85% on the day at $3.587/oz by the close.” Similarly, Deutsche Bank notes that silver “reversed a -6.51% intra-day decline to close +0.91% higher,” underscoring the sharp intraday swings across the complex. By contrast, the bank reports that “industrial metals did lose further ground, with copper (-0.61%) down to its lowest since December 2025,” extending the recent weakness in base metals.

Williams flags more work on inflation, keeps Fed tone firmly hawkish

Fed’s Williams delivers a speech that scores 6.2/10 on the FXS Speechtracker, exactly in line with the historical average, signaling a consistent hawkish stance rather than an escalation. The emphasis that the U.S. central bank “still has work to do” to bring inflation back to the 2% target, alongside projections of 3.5% inflation at end-2026 and a return to 2% only by 2028, underscores a prolonged restrictive bias even as the economy is described as strong, resilient and supported by a stable job market. Upside inflation risks, uncertainty around energy prices and AI, and a 2.75% growth outlook for 2026–2027 collectively point to a Fed that is not yet ready to pivot, a backdrop typically supportive of the Dollar on rate expectations.

The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rises by 0.35 points to 152.49, reinforcing that the overall policy tone remains deep in hawkish territory. The combination of an unchanged FXS Speechtracker score and a higher FXS Fed Sentiment Index level suggests that markets see Williams’ remarks as confirming entrenched hawkishness rather than introducing a new dovish tilt, a configuration that should keep Dollar bulls comfortable with the current Fed narrative.

Technical Analysis: Gold keeps a bearish vibe under the 100-day SMA

In the daily chart, XAU/USD extends a bearish phase as spot gold remains well under the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and below the Bollinger Bands’ 20-day middle band. The Relative Strength Index (14) sits at 31.21, hovering just above oversold territory and hinting at persistent selling pressure rather than a decisive exhaustion of the downtrend.

On the topside, initial resistance is located at the Bollinger middle band around $3,840, with stronger supply seen at the 100-day SMA at $4,160 and the Bollinger upper band near $4,230. On the downside, the Bollinger lower band at roughly $3,450 acts as the next notable support, and a sustained break below this floor would reinforce the bearish bias and open the door to further downside in the near term.

data.title: Indian Rupee Hits Pause After A Rally As Revived Hormuz Risks Boost Oil Prices
data.description:
• The Indian Rupee falls further against the US Dollar due to rising oil prices.

  • FIIs continuous buying in Indian stock market will likely limit the INR’s downside.

  • The RBI is almost certain to hike the Repo Rate next week.

The Indian Rupee (INR) extends correction further against the US Dollar (USD) on Friday. The USD/INR pair recovers further to near 92.95 as a sharp recovery in oil prices weighs on the Indian currency.

On Friday, the MCX Crude Oil contract expiring on December 18 extends its winning streak for the fourth trading day, rising over 2% to near Rs. 8,060.

Currencies from economies, such as India, which rely heavily on oil imports to meet their energy needs, tend to underperform in a high-oil-price environment.

Oil gains deepen as Strait of Hormuz risks intensify

Strategists at Scotiabank stress that the latest advance in crude is more than a routine bounce, arguing that “the gains are important, notable, and reflect the renewed barrage of worrisome headlines suggesting an intensification of Iranian strikes on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz.” They point to this escalation in geopolitical tension as a key driver of the move, reinforcing the market’s sensitivity to any disruption risks along this critical shipping corridor.

Continued FII buying likely limit INR’s downside

The continuous inflow of overseas funds into the Indian stock market will likely keep the downside in the Indian Rupee limited. So far in November, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) have remained net buyers in all complete trading days and raised their stake worth Rs. 1,27,944.79 crore.

The interest of FIIs into the Indian stock market as financial markets started looking beyond the global Artificial Intelligence (AI) trade, following the victory of Democrats in United States (US) midterm elections and corporate governance issues in giant chipmaker Nvidia.

RBI is almost certain to hike rates next week

Analysts at Deutsche Bank said, “With Consumer Price Index (CPI) now above tolerance band, underlying inflation broadening and real GDP growth likely to remain above 7% despite West Asia crisis, the bank expects Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to continue tightening.” Reuters reported. The bank added that there are also risks of a bigger RBI Repo Rate hike on December 4.

Technical Analysis: USD/INR stays below 20-day EMA

In the daily chart, USD/INR trades at 92.95, keeping a bearish near-term tone as it remains under the 20-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) at 93.52. The pair’s inability to reclaim this overhead EMA suggests rallies are still being capped by short-term trend resistance, while the Relative Strength Index (RSI) at 35.42 has bounced from oversold territory but stays below the mid-50s area, hinting at only modest stabilization rather than a decisive reversal.

On the topside, immediate resistance is located at the 20-day EMA near 93.52, and a sustained break above this level would be needed to ease current downside pressure and open the door for a broader corrective rebound. Looking down, the November 25 low at 92.18 is the key support level.

data.title: IBEX Elliott Wave Bearish Sequence Suggests Further Weakness Toward 18,400
data.description:
The IBEX continues to display a bearish Elliott Wave sequence from the August 13, 2026 high, favoring additional downside toward the 100% extension area near 18,400. The decline is unfolding as a double-three corrective structure, reinforcing the view that the broader correction remains incomplete. As shown on the 1-hour chart, wave ((w)) completed at 18,643.7 before the index staged a recovery in wave ((x)). That rebound reached 20,090.03 and completed the corrective phase. From there, sellers regained control, and the index resumed its decline in wave ((y)).

Importantly, the break below the wave ((w)) low confirms that the next bearish leg is already in progress. This development strengthens the view that the correction from the August peak still has room to extend lower. The current wave ((y)) is taking shape as a zigzag pattern in a lesser degree. Such a structure typically consists of three waves and often appears as the final component of a double-three correction.

Looking closer at the internal structure, wave (a) of ((y)) ended at 18,635.8 and unfolded as a clear five-wave impulse. This impulsive decline supports the bearish outlook and suggests that the broader corrective sequence remains active. Following the completion of wave (a), the index is now expected to develop a wave (b) rebound. This recovery should correct the cycle from the November 12, 2026 high before sellers re-emerge.

In the near term, any rally is expected to remain corrective in nature. As long as the pivot at 20,090.03 stays intact, rallies should fail in either a 3-swing or 7-swing structure. Consequently, the broader bearish sequence is expected to continue, keeping the focus on further weakness toward the 18,400 area and potentially lower levels thereafter.

data.title: Royal Bank Of Canada Forecast Ahead Of Earnings: Will It Rebound Or Fall?
data.description:
Royal Bank of Canada (RY) stock has dropped into a correction, moving from a record high of $306 in July to $269 today. This retreat has coincided with the ongoing weakness of Canadian and US banks. Focus now shifts to its earnings, which will come out on December 3.

RBC Bank is falling as global banks drop

Royal Bank of Canada, the biggest bank in Canada, is a top player that offers diverse services, including personal banking, commercial banking, wealth management, insurance, and capital markets. It has the biggest market share in the country, which helps it generate over $66 billion a year.

RBC stock has dropped recently because of the ongoing weakness in the banking industry. A closer look at most banks stocks shows that many of them have pulled back in the past few months. 

The most recent results showed that RBC’s business did well in the second quarter, with its revenue rising by 11% to $18.3 billion. The closely-watched net income rose to $6 billion, while the return on equity rose to 17.9%.

READ MORE: Royal Bank of Canada stock double-tops ahead of Q1 earnings

Most of its businesses did well during the quarter. For example, its wealth management division grew by 32% to $1.44 billion, helped by its higher fee-based assets. Its commercial banking revenue rose by 12% to $936 million, while its capital markets segment made $1.54 billion, up by 16% from a year earlier. 

These segments helped to offset the decline in its insurance and personal computing business. 

RBC to publish earnings next week

Therefore, looking ahead, the upcoming earnings report is expected to show that its business continued growing, driven by its wealth management division. 

The challenge, however, is that its capital markets business likely remained under pressure in the fourth fiscal quarter. This business has been relatively weak because of the rising interest rates. Indeed, a report by the London Stock Exchange showed that global deal value dropped by 41% in the third quarter to $993 billion. 

Most companies also published slower investment banking revenue. Morgan Stanley’s investment banking revenue rose by 2% to $2.16 billion, while Citigroup’s, JPMorgan, and Goldman Sachs grew by 9%, 15%, and 21%, respectively. 

Yahoo Finance data shows that analysts expect the upcoming earnings to show that its revenue rose by 7.37% to $18.48 billion. The earnings per share is expected to move to $4.15 from $3.85 in the same period last year. Investors will focus on its net income margin and its wealth management and investment banking business. Also, markets will react to its costs, which have been rising recently. Its non-interest expense rose by 6% in the third quarter.

Analysts have a muted outlook for the company. Scotiabank reiterated its outperform rating, while Barclays maintained its overweight position. TD Securities also maintained a buy rating, while Raymond James downgraded its rating from outperform to market outperform. The average target among analysts on its US shares is $227, up by 20% from the current level.

The daily chart shows that the Royal Bank of Canada share price has been under pressure in the past few months. It dropped from $306 in June to the current $268. 

The stock has now settled along the 23.6% Fibonacci Retracement level, which also coincides with the lowest level on October 8. It has dropped below the 50-day Exponential Moving Average (EMA) and the Supertrend indicator.

data.title: Is Oracle The Next Bear Stearns?
data.description:
The Bear Stearns Comparison

On Thanksgiving night, Michael Burry shared a piece with a striking comparison. In its November 20 analysis, Groundbreaker reported that five-year default protection on Oracle cost more than comparable protection on Bear Stearns at the start of 2008.

Groundbreaker’s argument starts with the rent. A developer borrows against what a tenant has promised to pay for a data center. If lenders grow less confident in that tenant, they’ll lend less against the same lease. Take a campus valued at $100 million with $85 million of debt. A 15% drop in its value wipes out the owner’s equity on paper. That can make the next campus harder to finance even if the tenant is still paying on time.

Three Days Versus Three Years

Bear Stearns borrowed against mortgage bonds, much of it overnight. As major lenders stopped renewing those loans, its pool of available cash and liquid assets went from about $18 billion on Monday to $2 billion on Thursday, as shown in a study of the run. That Thursday, it told the Fed it expected to come up short the next day.

Oracle, meanwhile, sold $10 billion in bonds and $10 billion in common stock on November 4. It agreed to pay 7% to 8.65% interest on the bonds, and the earliest of those bonds comes due in 2029, according to its SEC filing. On November 20, the same day Groundbreaker published, Oracle said it had secured the money it needed to fulfill its contract with OpenAI.

Oracle paid up for time and brought in new shareholders to bear part of the risk. It still needs OpenAI to pay for the computing capacity it signed up for. If those payments fall short, Oracle will owe the same interest on its new bonds with less cash coming in.

Who Has To Sell?

The places to look for a 2008-style run are the lenders and funds holding the debt. A lender with long-term funding may be able to hold a troubled loan while the borrower restructures. A fund facing margin calls or withdrawals may have to sell whatever it can, including investments unrelated to AI. Fed Governor Michael Barr singled out leveraged funds as a potential source of forced selling in an AI downturn.

Some losses could also land with the tech companies that helped finance their customers. At a TeraWulf campus in Kentucky, Google agreed to step in if Anthropic defaults on certain data-center leases. Google can pay the overdue rent and take over the lease or, in some circumstances, pay an exit fee. That protection kicks in when the last data hall on the relevant lease starts its term, according to TeraWulf’s filing.

For stock investors, we’d watch two things. First, are companies postponing campuses and chip orders as financing gets more expensive? That matters to Nvidia and its suppliers. Second, are lenders pulling funding from firms that hold AI debt? That’s how trouble at a data center can reach stocks that have nothing to do with AI.

Where We’re Looking Next

CoreWeave looks vulnerable if financing gets tighter. It spent $9.4 billion on capital investment in the third quarter and generated about $2 billion in operating cash flow, according to its latest earnings release.

We’re still bullish on AI names with stronger balance sheets. We’ve lined up a potential trade for today in one company we think could soon get an investment from the U.S. government.

data.title: HPE Plunges Despite Raising The Bar For 2027
data.description:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise delivered exactly what the bulls were looking for after a punishing month for AI hardware: a clean beat, an above-the-range quarter, and a fiscal 2027 outlook that blew past where analysts had been modeling.

The stock's reaction was more complicated. Shares rallied 17% during Monday's regular session as technology stocks surged, then gave back all of the gain – and then some – to drop below $40 per share in early Wednesday trading.

A Beat on Every Line That Matters

Adjusted earnings came in at $1.43 per share, topping the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $1.29 by nearly 11% and clearing the top of management's own $1.20 to $1.30 range. That compares with $0.62 a year ago. Revenue rose 50% to $14.55 billion, edging past consensus, and HPE has now topped the Zacks consensus on earnings in each of the last four quarters.

Fiscal 2026 as a whole was transformational. Revenue grew 36% to $46.7 billion, adjusted earnings reached $3.97 per share, and free cash flow climbed to $4.5 billion from less than $1 billion the year before. Antonio Neri described HPE as "a fundamentally different company, with greater earnings power," and the numbers certainly back up the corporate language.

The Guidance Is the Story

The fourth quarter was good. The fiscal 2027 outlook was something else entirely. In September, management laid out a framework calling for revenue growth of 13% to 17% and earnings growth of 16% to 20%. On Monday evening, the company raised revenue growth to 27% to 35%, or $59.4 billion to $63.1 billion, and set adjusted EPS at $5.05 to $5.35.

Put those numbers next to the Street. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2027 stood at $4.74 per share on $55.12 billion in revenue, so the low end of the new range sits about 6.5% above consensus and the midpoint nearly 10% above it. First-quarter guidance of $1.30 to $1.40 compares with a consensus of $1.10. The midpoint of the annual range implies growth of about 31% on top of a year in which earnings nearly doubled.

Expect estimate revisions to move sharply higher over the next week, which is precisely the dynamic the Zacks Rank rewards; HPE (HPE - Free Report) entered the report as a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).

Servers Carried the Quarter

Server revenue nearly doubled, up 94.7% to $8.8 billion, as the hyperscaler inferencing deal and the AI systems backlog converted to shipments. By my arithmetic, servers accounted for close to 90% of the company's year-over-year revenue increase and roughly 60% of total revenue.

Networking, the segment management has been touting, grew a more modest 12.3% to $3.1 billion, toward the top of management's 11% to 13% guide. Security slipped 1.8%. Networking operating margin eased to 22.1% from 23.4% a year ago.

The forward indicators were stronger: networking orders more than doubled, and networks-for-AI orders hit a record $1.2 billion in the quarter, with Neri putting the fiscal-year total in the "mid-$2 billion" range, inside the target he set. For fiscal 2027, management is targeting $7.5 billion to $8 billion of cumulative networks-for-AI orders, weighted to the back half as AMD Helios and Oracle deployments ramp.

None of that is a problem. But the segment outlook management gave on the call confirms that the 2027 upgrade leans more heavily on AI compute than on the Juniper pivot: Cloud & AI revenue is guided to grow 30% to 40%, against high-teens to low-20s growth for networking. Server demand is the more cyclical of the two.

Margins Held Up Better Than Feared

The margin picture is a quiet win. Non-GAAP gross margin stepped down to 38.2% from a record 40.4% in the third quarter, which was expected given the size and mix of the hyperscaler shipments, but it was still up 180 basis points from a year ago. More telling, Cloud & AI operating margin reached 18.4%, double the 9.3% of a year earlier and well above the mid-teens rate management had flagged.

The catch came on the call. Management guided Cloud & AI operating margin to about 14% for fiscal 2027, well below the 18.4% just reported, and said gross margin should moderate as the year progresses, driven by mix and the timing of large AI systems ramps. Marie Myers was candid: "we do expect to see some pressure in pricing."

Why the Stock Slipped

The post-release slide has a clearer explanation. The 17% Monday-session rally front-ran much of the good news, and the call then introduced two less comfortable details.


Image Source: StockCharts

The first is the margin step-down described above. The second came from a J.P. Morgan question: spread evenly, the fiscal 2027 networks-for-AI order target implies roughly flat quarterly orders versus the $1.2 billion just booked.

Management pointed to scale-out, scale-across and Helios networking trays as upside, but the arithmetic is fair. Neither undermines the guidance, but both temper how far investors should extrapolate one blockbuster quarter.

Bottom Line

At under $40, HPE trades at less than nine times the midpoint of its fiscal 2027 earnings guidance, a multiple that still prices in a great deal of skepticism.

Neri made the point himself on the call: "I don't see us at a multiple that is 8x-9x." The concentration in servers and the coming margin moderation are legitimate reasons for some caution. But a record $10.5 billion AI backlog, orders up 88%, a guide well above consensus and rising cash returns, all at a single-digit multiple, is not a stock I would be selling into this week’s downturn.

data.title: Shopify Stock Is Still Under Pressure: Is It A Buy As Valuation Concerns Persist?
data.description:
Shopify (SHOP) stock price has plunged into a bear market, moving from the October high of $181 to the current $133. It has slumped below key moving averages, a trend that continued after releasing its earnings report, which showed that its revenue growth slowed during the quarter.

Shopify’s revenue growth is slowing 

SHOP stock has plunged into a bear market, moving from a high of $180 in October to the current $133. This retreat continued after the company published its financial results, which showed that its revenue growth was slowing.

Shopify said that its revenue rose to $3.7 billion in the third quarter from $2.8 billion in the same period last year. Most of this revenue was in its merchant solutions, with the rest being in its subscription solutions.

The company's net income jumped from $264 million in the third quarter of last year to $462 million. 

However, there are signs that other parts of the business are slowing, with its global merchandise volume remaining at 30% in the last three consecutive quarters. Its European GMV dropped from 42% in the second quarter of 2024 to 33%, with the North American figure remaining at 28%.

Analysts expect the company's revenue growth will remain under pressure in the coming quarters. The average estimate among analysts is that its fourth-quarter revenue is expected to come in at $4.6 billion, up by 31.1% from the same period last year.

If the estimate is correct, the annual revenue will come in at $15.3 billion, up by 32.50% from the same period last year. This growth will then slow to 26% next year to $19.3 billion, which is quite good for a company that has been in the business for two decades.

Shopify is benefiting from the market share of its business, since it is the biggest name in the e-commerce software industry. Most recently, there is hope that it will benefit from the rise of AI agents, which are now able to shop for people. As these agents become more popular, they will lead to more shopping activity over time.

Shopify valuation concerns remains 

The main challenge facing the SHOP stock is that its business has always been highly overvalued because of its growing market share, revenue and profitability growth, and its ability to continue monetizing its products.

Shopify has a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 70, and a forward PEG multiple of 2.19. In contrast, the S&P 500 Index has a multiple of 17, while the technology median is 18.2. These numbers are also higher than other companies, including retailers like Walmart and Costco.

The only valuation multiple that can justify Shopify’s current price is the Rule-of-40, which looks at a company’s revenue growth and its margins. By adding these two numbers, Shopify has a multiple of 47%, which is higher than the key level of 40.

Analysts have a bullish outlook for the stock. Argus reiterated the buy rating and set a target of $180, while Bernstein has a target of $165. Other analysts who are bullish on the company are from Needham, Wells Fargo, and UBS Group.

Shopify stock price technical analysis 

The daily chart shows that Shopify stock has dropped sharply since mid-October, moving from a high of $180 to the current $133.

Shopify has already dropped below the ascending trendline that connects the lowest swings since May 14 this year.

The stock has also dropped below the 50-day and 200-day moving averages and is now hovering between the 50% and 61.8% Fibonacci retracement level.

Therefore, the stock will likely remain under pressure for a while and possibly retest the support at $100 and then bounce back, possibly to $150 in the future.

data.title: These 3 Retail Stocks Are Best Positioned To Benefit From Thanksgiving In 2026
data.description:
The Thanksgiving shopping rush looks a little smaller this year.

The National Retail Federation estimates 182.7 million consumers plan to shop between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, down from 186.9 million last year.

Black Friday alone is expected to draw 126 million shoppers.

With more consumers starting early, the retailers best positioned to benefit are the ones giving shoppers several reasons to spend across the weekend.

Walmart can turn a grocery trip into a gift purchase, Target is using exclusives to bring people into stores, and Amazon (AMZN) is putting deals inside a football broadcast.

Walmart can turn a $35 dinner into a bigger shopping basket

Walmart (WMT) advertised a 26-item Thanksgiving meal basket for $35 that serves 10. At $3.5 a person, the offer gives households a concrete reason to choose it for one of November’s biggest grocery trips.

The payoff can come from what shoppers add to the order, from roasting pans and extra desserts to toys they were already planning to buy.

Walmart’s main Black Friday sale went online Nov. 23, overlapping with the final days of Thanksgiving prep.

In-store deals begin Friday morning. That timing matters because Walmart’s US e-commerce sales rose 23% in its latest quarter.

A customer who orders groceries online can browse holiday deals in the same place, giving Walmart another chance to win the gift purchase before that shopper opens a rival’s app.

Target gives Black Friday shoppers a reason to show up

Target (TGT) has $30 Thanksgiving meal for six but the bigger opportunity comes Friday morning. The first 100 eligible shoppers at each store get a gift card, with one card per location worth $1,000.

Target is also rolling out exclusive Pokémon and Topps trading-card products. A giveaway can get people through the door. An exclusive gives them something to buy that they can’t easily price-check at a rival.

Target enters the weekend with store comparable sales up 4.6% in its latest quarter.

The question for investors is how much of that traffic turns into a fuller cart. A shopper who comes for a collectible and leaves with holiday décor, wrapping paper or another gift makes the promotion more valuable than the giveaway alone would suggest.

Amazon brings the sale to the football audience

Amazon’s (AMZN) holiday sale runs through Nov. 30, with two rounds of featured deals on both Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Its most distinctive sales pitch comes during Friday’s Pittsburgh Steelers–Denver Broncos game on Prime Video.

Viewers can use their remote or the Amazon Shopping app to see featured deals and buy merchandise during the broadcast, giving Amazon a chance to reach people who tuned in for football and may never have planned to browse a sale.

That extra attention has value beyond the items Amazon sells directly. Independent merchants can pay Amazon for services such as fulfillment, and brands can pay for ad placements.

For investors, that means a busy shopping weekend can generate revenue for Amazon even when another merchant makes the sale.

data.title: When A Stock Falls, Is The Business Really In Trouble?
data.description:
When a stock falls, has the business weakened or has the price come back in line with earnings? Chuck Carnevale uses FAST Graphs to show how earnings growth, cash flow, and the price you pay can shape long-term returns.

When a Stock Falls, Is the Business Really in Trouble?

A falling stock price tells you what investors are willing to pay today. To understand what the business is worth, look at what it earns, how much cash it generates, and what you can reasonably expect it to earn in the future.

In this FAST Graphs video, Chuck Carnevale demonstrates a simple way to start. He takes the stock price off the chart and looks at how the business performed on its own. Then he puts the price back on the chart to see where it tracked earnings and where it pulled away. It’s a practical application of a theme from All Investing Is Value Investing, the book Chuck co-authored with Professor Nathan Mauck.

A strong business can still be an expensive stock

Oracle (ORCL) and Amgen (AMGN) both grew earnings through difficult economic periods. Yet the returns Chuck shows vary widely depending on what an investor paid. In one Amgen example, buying at a lower valuation produced a higher annualized return than buying at a premium during a period of faster earnings growth. The starting price mattered enough to outweigh the difference in growth.

Alphabet (GOOGL) illustrates another point. Change the time frame on a FAST Graphs chart and the historical earnings growth rate can change with it. That can shift the valuation reference. Comparing several periods helps you see whether a particular growth rate reflects a sustained record or an unusually strong stretch.

Do the numbers support the business story?

Copart (CPRT) offers a concrete example of a competitive advantage. Its salvage yards and insurer relationships bring vehicles to auction, and a global network of buyers makes those auctions more valuable to insurers. Each side helps attract the other. That explains why the business has been hard to replicate. The valuation question is how much to pay for that advantage if future earnings grow more slowly than they did in the past.

Chuck asks a similar question about NVIDIA (NVDA). Using Ask Charles, he looks at how NVIDIA’s CUDA software ecosystem supports its competitive position and what the company’s balance sheet and cash generation say about the business. The valuation still depends on whether NVIDIA can deliver the earnings growth investors expect.

What does it take to recover from a 50% loss?

If a $100 investment falls to $50, it takes a 100% gain to get back to $100. Even a 30% rally would bring it only to $65. That’s why the size of a rebound tells you so little on its own. The price you paid and the earnings the business can deliver still matter.

Watch the full video to see how Chuck uses FAST Graphs to compare earnings and stock prices, weigh growth expectations, and look for a margin of safety.

  • The FCC approved SpaceX’s plan to deploy up to one million AI satellites.

SpaceX stock Nasdaq: SPCX surged nearly 7.5% in overnight trading on Friday after Elon Musk expanded his commitment to distribute shares to American children.

The shares gained 7.47% on alternative trading platform Blue Ocean ATS, according to CNBC. SpaceX had closed 1.3% higher at $127.44 on Wednesday, ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

Elon Musk's latest pledge comes as the company secures regulatory approval for an ambitious orbital data centre project and accelerates investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Elon Musk's giveaway could create a generation of shareholders

Elon Musk has pledged to give American children an additional SpaceX share annually, extending an initial giveaway estimated to be worth around $18 billion.

SpaceX announced on Wednesday that it would issue one Class A share to each currently active Trump Account, with Musk personally matching the company's contribution.

The corporate distribution is expected in December, while Musk's personal contribution is scheduled for June 2027, following the expiration of his share lock-up period.

Assuming 72 million children receive one share annually, Musk's recurring donation would be worth approximately $9.2 billion at Wednesday's closing price. However, the actual value would depend on eligibility and prevailing market prices.

“What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base,” Christopher Brankin, global markets adviser at Mitrade Group, told Reuters.

For existing shareholders, the distinction between the two contributions matters. Newly issued corporate shares dilute existing ownership, whereas transfers from Musk's personal holdings do not increase the outstanding share count.

Orbital data centres could reshape SpaceX stock's growth prospects

Beyond the giveaway, SpaceX secured permission from the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy up to one million satellites for its proposed Starmind orbital computing network.

The project could eventually reduce dependence on terrestrial electricity networks by using solar energy to power computing infrastructure in space.

SpaceX must begin deployment by November 2033 and deploy at least 100,000 satellites by November 2035 under the regulatory authorisation.

Its rocket manufacturing and launch capabilities could give the company an advantage over competitors that rely on external launch providers.

Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu described SpaceX's launch business as its “core competitive advantage”, according to Investing.com. The brokerage initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a $210 price target on Monday.

Meanwhile, the company's terrestrial computing expansion continues.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs announced the pricing of approximately $44 billion in financing for graphics processors and related equipment last week.

However, the orbital project's commercial viability remains unproven, with considerable engineering and financing challenges ahead.

SpaceX stock today: Wall Street sees substantial upside

SpaceX remains below its June initial public offering price of $135, based on Wednesday's regular-session close, despite strong earnings growth.

Third-quarter revenue increased 161% to $14.6 billion, while the company reported net income of $4.4 billion against a loss of $1.1 billion a year earlier.

Baron Capital founder Ron Baron believes SpaceX's data centres could generate more than $50 billion in annual rental revenue, according to Benzinga.

The average price target of $265 among analysts tracked by TipRanks implies approximately 108% upside from Wednesday's close.

data.title: Thanksgiving Inflation, The Fed’s Debt Trap, And Gold’s Eastward Shift
data.description:
In the latest Money Metals Midweek Memo, host Mike Maharrey connects the rising cost of Thanksgiving dinner to a larger problem facing the U.S. economy: persistent inflation, record debt, and a Federal Reserve caught between fighting rising prices and keeping a debt-heavy economy afloat.

Maharrey also examines the recent sell-off in gold and silver, the scramble for liquidity on Wall Street, and surging Chinese gold demand. His central argument is that short-term pressure on precious metals has not erased gold’s long-term case.

Thanksgiving Dinner Costs Rise 6% in 2026

A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people is expected to cost an average of $58.63 this year, about 6% more than in 2025, according to the Farm Bureau. The organization has tracked grocery prices for 40 years, using hundreds of volunteers in all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

That increase is nearly double the roughly 3.5% inflation rate measured by the Consumer Price Index, Maharrey noted. It also ends a three-year trend of falling Thanksgiving meal costs.

The longer-term comparison looks different. Since 2012, the cost of a traditional Thanksgiving dinner has risen about 18.5%, while cumulative CPI inflation has reached roughly 49%. Since October 2021, food prices in the CPI’s “food at home” index have climbed 22%, compared with an increase of about 10% for the traditional Thanksgiving meal.

Maharrey said the difference reflects how inflation moves unevenly across the economy. Supply and demand affect individual prices, while grocery stores may discount turkey and other holiday staples to bring customers in. Those changing prices can coexist with a general rise in the overall price level.

Inflation Compounds Even When It Cools

Maharrey cautioned that slower inflation does not mean prices are falling. It means they are rising at a slower pace. Even the Federal Reserve’s 2% inflation target compounds over time, steadily reducing the purchasing power of money.

Inflation, Maharrey argued, has remained above 2% for 68 consecutive months. He questioned whether policymakers can bring it down to target without damaging an economy weighed down by government, corporate, and consumer debt.

The debate has become central to the outlook for gold and silver. Maharrey said market commentary has focused on expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates in December and keep rates higher for longer. He argued that this view often overlooks the strain higher borrowing costs place on an already indebted economy.

The Federal Reserve’s Inflation and Debt Dilemma

The episode framed the policy debate as a Fed “catch-22.” Higher interest rates may help restrain inflation, but they also make it more expensive to service debt and can put pressure on businesses and consumers.

Maharrey cited U.S. national debt above $40.5 trillion, with the total approaching $40.7 trillion and potentially reaching $41 trillion within the next month or two. He also pointed to more than $1 trillion in annual federal interest expense, rising small-business bankruptcies, and consumers struggling with high-interest credit card debt.

Billionaire hedge fund manager Bill Ackman has warned that continued rate hikes could push the United States into recession. In a post on X, Ackman called further increases another mistake and said financial conditions had already tightened sharply. Maharrey cited SpaceX securing debt financing at 8.25%, compared with a 6% rate on its unsecured bond offering at the time of its IPO in June.

Maharrey also cited small-business bankruptcies rising 46% during the first nine months of 2026 and an increase in delinquent auto loans as signs of financial strain. In his view, rate hikes could intensify pressure across an economy carrying heavy debt loads.

Ackman has argued that a 3% inflation target may be more realistic in a world shaped by geopolitical risk, military spending, tariffs, deglobalization, and investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure and energy. Maharrey challenged the idea that a higher target solves inflation, arguing that it would instead accept a faster loss of purchasing power.

Years of Easy Money Complicate the Fed’s Choices

Maharrey traced the current dilemma to years of monetary stimulus. After the 2008 financial crisis, the Federal Reserve held rates near zero for almost a decade. A limited attempt to normalize rates in 2018 was followed by rate cuts and renewed quantitative easing.

By the time the COVID-19 pandemic began, the Fed had already cut rates three times and expanded its balance sheet. During the pandemic, it brought rates back to zero and injected nearly $5 trillion into the economy through quantitative easing.

When the Fed began raising rates in March 2022, the change helped trigger a banking crisis, Maharrey said. He argued that this history shows how difficult it may be to withdraw monetary support without causing significant economic stress.

Maharrey believes that, when forced to choose between fighting inflation and supporting the economy during a crisis, the Federal Reserve has historically chosen stimulus. He expects the central bank could eventually cut rates and expand money creation again, even if that means renewed inflationary pressure.

Why Gold and Silver Have Fallen

Gold was trading below $3,500 an ounce as Maharrey recorded the episode, nearly $2,000 below its January high. He described himself as short-term bearish on precious metals, while maintaining that the growing debt burden supports gold’s longer-term outlook.

One factor behind the sell-off, he said, is a scramble for liquidity. As investors sell assets to raise cash, gold and silver can fall alongside stocks, even though precious metals are often viewed as safe havens. Investors may sell highly liquid gold to cover margin calls or exit losing trades.

Maharrey pointed to similar behavior during the early stages of the 2008 financial crisis and the pandemic. In his view, gold’s initial decline during market stress does not necessarily signal that its safe-haven role has disappeared.

Chinese Gold Demand Surges as Western Investors Sell

While Western investors have been selling, Chinese buyers have continued accumulating gold. China imported 155.9 metric tons in October, up 174% from October 2025. The value of China’s gold imports reached a record $29 billion so far in 2026, and gold was the country’s third-largest import category in October.

Gold withdrawals from the Shanghai Gold Exchange also strengthened during a month when they typically ease. Withdrawals rose 2% month over month to 94 tons in October, according to the World Gold Council. Maharrey said dip buying and strong bullion sales helped drive the increase.

He also noted speculation that higher gold imports could help reduce the appearance of China’s large trade surplus by increasing the value of imports. More broadly, he described a pattern in which price weakness in Western markets has coincided with continued gold accumulation in China and India.

Trading-hour data cited in the episode showed gold rising 12.9% during Asian trading hours in the first six months of the year, while falling 15% during North American trading hours. Gold declined 1.3% during European hours over the same period. Maharrey said the pattern points to a shift in gold flows from Western markets toward Asia, where new infrastructure is also being developed to challenge Western dominance in gold trading.

Maharrey’s Outlook: Short-Term Volatility, Long-Term Inflation Risk

Maharrey’s outlook combines caution about the near term with a bullish long-term view of gold. Precious metals may remain under pressure as investors seek liquidity and markets respond to interest-rate expectations. But he argues that heavy debt, the limits of monetary tightening, and the possibility of renewed stimulus continue to support gold’s long-term role as an inflation hedge.

As the holiday season begins, Maharrey also highlighted gold and silver as potential gifts, describing them as tangible assets that can be held over time. He directed listeners to Money Metals for precious metals products, market news, and information about buying, selling, and storing bullion.

data.title: AI Off-Balance Sheet Financing Worries The Fed
data.description:
The October FOMC minutes contain a sentence worth discussing. Per the recently released minutes, the Federal Reserve staff :

highlighted the rapid growth of debt associated with the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, noting that off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing arrangements among AI-related firms could amplify losses if returns on AI investment were to disappoint.

We wrote about the circular financing half of that sentence two weeks ago in Nvidia Circular Financing. The leasing half deserves equal attention and has received very little media coverage.

Here is the leasing mechanism that worries the Fed. When a hyperscaler commits to a long-dated data center lease, accounting rules do not recognize the obligation until the lease commences. A company can therefore sign binding commitments for facilities that will not open for years and record no liability until then. They will disclose the future obligation in a footnote.

The leasing commitments are not small. Reporting on the filings of the five largest US hyperscalers puts combined future data center lease commitments nearing $1 trillion, of which roughly two-thirds sits off balance sheet. Meta alone discloses about $279 billion, none of it on its balance sheet, alongside a $28 billion residual value guarantee on leases beginning in 2029 that is also unrecorded.

So why should we care? Consider that the massive AI buildout is driving the economy today and promises significant future growth. The buildout is predicated on massive capital spending. This spending is increasingly coming from investors, not from cash flows. These investors should be aware that almost every financial leverage measure analysts, index providers, and rating agencies apply to these companies is calculated from balance sheets that omit most of the commitments.

The Fed minutes further noted:

Greater scrutiny of the sector’s returns and financing could lead to a slowing in AI-related spending.

The Fed appears to be contemplating a credit crunch if investors were to hold back on AI investments and the economic impact it could have on the entire economy.

What To Watch Today

Market Trading Update

On Wednesday, we used Nvidia’s round trip to explain the math of losses and noted that Monday’s 4.7% surge stalled just below the 200-day moving average. Today, I want to look underneath the index because market breadth is improving beneath a sloppy tape, and that matters more heading into December.

Last Friday was a genuine washout. Only 975 US-listed issues advanced against 4,014 decliners, and roughly 87% of dollar volume traded on the downside. The S&P 500 closed nearly three standard deviations below its 20-day average with RSI near 25.

Monday flipped that almost exactly, with 4,099 advancers, 655 decliners, and about 89% of dollar volume flowing into rising stocks. Paul Desmond’s work at Lowry Research tied pairs of 90% down days and 90% up days to selling climaxes. We came close to that pattern, though not quite.

Notice what happened next. The S&P 500 slipped on Tuesday and Wednesday, yet advancers beat decliners on both days, by nearly 3-to-1 on Wednesday. The catch is dollar volume. Only 38% and 42% of it flowed into rising stocks because the selling was concentrated in the mega-caps. To wit: the Nasdaq 100 briefly approached bear-market territory on Wednesday as Nvidia fell another 5%, while the S&P 400 midcaps gained about 1%.

The equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP) tells the story most clearly. It has reclaimed its 50-day moving average and sits only about 3% below its November 4 record high. The cap-weighted index, by contrast, remains roughly 8% off its October high and below its 200-day average near 7,348. Bob Farrell’s Rule #7 holds that broad markets are strong markets and narrow ones are fragile. Right now, the average stock is healing faster than the index, which is the opposite of a market that is breaking down.

Of course, the skeptic in the back row will point out that bear-market rallies also start with big up days. He’s right. Such is the problem with oversold bounces, since they all look identical on day one. The test I’m watching is Marty Zweig’s breadth thrust. The 10-day average of advancing stocks is near 40%, the launch point. A move above 61.5% within 10 sessions, which takes us into early December, would confirm that buyers are committing and not just covering shorts.

Here’s how we’re managing it. We trimmed technology on Tuesday and raised cash, and we are NOT chasing a holiday half-day with thin liquidity. We will redeploy in stages once the S&P 500 closes above its 200-day average and breadth confirms, favoring broad, equal-weight exposure over buying back the mega-cap “dip”. Friday’s low near 6,882 is the risk line. A close below it voids the healing thesis, and we will respect that.

The most convincing rallies are often the ones that fail.

The Black Friday Consumer Test

Consumer sentiment sits near a record low while consumers keep spending. The University of Michigan index registered 48.0 in October, the second weakest reading in the survey’s history, yet retail sales are running roughly 5% above last year. Black Friday will test which signal deserves more weight.

For starters, the hard data has held up much better than the consumer surveys. As we share below, other than in June and July, when consumers were shocked by higher gasoline prices, consumer spending has held up well. With rapidly declining gasoline prices, household confidence should improve and, with it, spending may pick up, including on Black Friday.

Forecasters cannot agree on what will happen this weekend. The National Retail Federation expects 182.7 million Thanksgiving weekend shoppers, fewer than last year. The International Council of Shopping Centers expects 237 million shoppers spending less, roughly $124 billion against $127 billion. Bain projects weekend sales up nearly 9%, and Adobe sees online spending rising 7.4%. Those are not small disagreements.

It is worth disclaiming that many consumers have already begun holiday shopping, so a meaningful share of the spending season has been pulled forward. A soft Friday may reflect timing rather than weakness, and a strong one may simply be borrowing from December.

Here is what we take from it. Sentiment surveys have insisted the consumer has been exhausted for well over a year, while spending carried on regardless. Until the hard data breaks, we would keep weighting what households do above what they say.

The Indian Rupee (INR) extends its correction further against the US Dollar (USD) on Friday. The USD/INR pair recovers further to near 92.75 as a sharp recovery in oil prices weighs on the Indian currency.

On Friday, the MCX Crude Oil contract expiring on December 18 extends its winning streak for the fourth trading day, rising 1.5% to near Rs. 8,000.

Currencies from economies, such as India, which rely heavily on oil imports to meet their energy needs, tend to underperform in a high-oil-price environment.

Oil gains deepen as Strait of Hormuz risks intensify

Strategists at Scotiabank stress that the latest advance in crude is more than a routine bounce, arguing that “the gains are important, notable, and reflect the renewed barrage of worrisome headlines suggesting an intensification of Iranian strikes on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz.” They point to this escalation in geopolitical tension as a key driver of the move, reinforcing the market’s sensitivity to any disruption risks along this critical shipping corridor.
