data.title: No Groundhog Day, No Cold Turkey: Wall Street's Thanksgiving Bounce Gives The AI Bulls Something To Chew On
data.description:
No Groundhog Day, and Thankfully No Cold Turkey

No Groundhog Day, and thankfully no cold turkey either. Investors appear to have used Thanksgiving as an opportunity to treat this week’s apparent double bottom as a chance for retail to continue rummaging through the carnage and pick up a few cheap AI stocks for their portfolios. After a November that has put even the most hardened technology bulls through the wringer, the hope is that the underlying fundamentals will eventually reassert themselves and, more importantly, that the worst of the liquidation has finally run its course.

That is certainly a more encouraging proposition than another day of watching the Nasdaq surrender an early recovery and head straight back into the basement. But I wouldn’t get too carried away with Thursday’s price action. With US cash markets closed and much of Wall Street operating with holiday staffing, the overseas session feels like a pass-the-rally-baton day rather than a genuine test of institutional conviction. I suspect a fair number of senior traders and risk managers have already called it a week and won’t be back at their desks until Monday.

Nonetheless, the market’s willingness to look beyond the immediate carnage is encouraging. Investors in Europe and Asia took their cue from Wednesday’s late recovery on Wall Street, when bargain hunters dragged the Nasdaq 100 back from the brink of a bear market after another extraordinary session of intraday swings.

But as I’ve been suggesting, the underlying market data tell a more interesting story. The pre-Thanksgiving turnaround and the overnight extension appear to be getting an additional lift from the unwinding of US equity downside hedges, creating a mechanical bid through the derivatives market as dealers adjust their bearish exposures. That is not only helping restore risk appetite but also putting a bid under the “ Big Board” sectors that have been under the cosh.

But there’s an important distinction between a rally driven by hedging-flow unwinds and one supported by genuine institutional buying. The former can move markets significantly, particularly when liquidity is thin, but the real test comes when Wall Street’s skeleton-thin holiday desks return to full force.

Europe’s Stoxx 600 rallied 1.7%, while the MSCI Asia Pacific Index climbed 0.8%, marking only its second advance in eleven sessions. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures added about 0.5%, suggesting that, for now at least, investors are willing to give the rebound the benefit of the doubt.

The improvement was particularly evident across Asian technology markets. South Korea’s SK Hynix (SKHY) and Japan’s Kioxia outperformed, while technology-heavy benchmarks in Taiwan and South Korea advanced more than 2%. European technology shares also gained more than 2%, although the broader regional rally was led by automobile manufacturers and mining stocks.

For South Korea, the timing of Wall Street’s rebound could hardly have been better. Seoul had already been scrambling to contain the fallout from the US-led rout in AI and semiconductor shares, with authorities temporarily easing daily corporate share-buyback limits for three months starting November 24 and launching an intensified crackdown on illegal short selling. The measures stopped short of an outright short-selling ban or direct government purchases of equities, despite short-selling turnover reaching roughly 23 trillion won between November 2 and 20, with foreign investors accounting for more than 75% of the activity.

Fortunately for Seoul, the Wall Street recovery gave Korean shares a timely lift before investors had much opportunity to test the latest page in the country’s ongoing plunge-protection playbook.

Regardless, that’s a reasonably constructive response to Wednesday’s late buying, especially after the beating technology investors have absorbed since the US midterm elections. Leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA) added another layer of uncertainty to an already uncomfortable market, pushing major equity benchmarks into correction territory and leaving traders struggling to distinguish a genuine recovery from another short-lived bounce.

At least Thursday’s response suggests the selling pressure has eased. Whether that translates into a sustained recovery is another matter, especially when much of the Wall Street crowd that normally sets the tone is probably more interested in turkey and football than adjusting its risk limits.

Sentiment Took the Beating. The Fundamentals May Have Survived.

A more constructive argument emerging from the wreckage is that investors spent much of November punishing technology shares for risks that haven’t materially changed underlying earnings and the investment outlook.

AI capital expenditure remains substantial, access to financing has not disappeared, and pricing power across some of the industry’s most important companies remains exceptionally strong. The damage has been concentrated in investor confidence, positioning and valuations rather than a wholesale deterioration in the businesses themselves.

That is essentially the case the bargain hunters are making.

After such a sharp adjustment in technology valuations, investors are beginning to ask whether the selling has gone too far relative to the earnings outlook. And if the answer is yes, then the market doesn’t necessarily need a spectacular new catalyst to recover. Sometimes it simply needs the forced sellers to finish selling and the remaining investors to rediscover a little confidence.

The apparent double bottom has therefore arrived at an interesting moment. Wednesday’s recovery didn’t erase November’s damage, but it suggested buyers are becoming more willing to absorb supply rather than stand aside and wait for another leg lower.

There are also some encouraging signs beyond technology. Copper recovered nearly 1% from an eleven-month low, Brent crude climbed above $96 a barrel for the first time in more than a week, and European government bonds weakened as demand for traditional havens eased.

Those moves suggest the improved risk appetite isn’t confined to a handful of semiconductor names. The participation of cyclical shares and commodities gives the rebound more credibility, although one holiday session is hardly enough evidence to declare the correction finished.

And therein lies the distinction. Fundamentals don’t need to have deteriorated for the market to have fallen too far, but a recovery in sentiment doesn't automatically mean the coast is clear.

The Fed Hasn’t Gone Away for Thanksgiving

Despite the renewed enthusiasm around the AI trade, one rather awkward guest is still at the Thanksgiving table: the Federal Reserve.

The prospect of another interest-rate increase in December remains a headwind for equities, particularly after a month in which investors have been repeatedly reminded that higher financing costs and crowded positioning can be an uncomfortable combination.

The S&P 500 is threatening to match one of its choppiest trading stretches since the 2022 bear market, and while Wednesday’s recovery was impressive, nothing obvious changed the outlook. Buyers simply emerged late in the session, apparently deciding that the damage had become excessive.

That is not necessarily a bad thing. Markets frequently turn before the news improves, and waiting for an official invitation to buy usually means arriving after everybody else has taken the best seats.

But it does leave the recovery with something to prove.

For now, the credit market has held up well enough to suggest equity volatility hasn’t developed into a broader financial problem. That is encouraging, particularly while economic growth and corporate earnings remain reasonably resilient. If the Fed ends its tightening cycle next year, there is still a plausible path to further equity gains.

The immediate difficulty is that the Fed hasn’t finished its work, and the latest technology rebound has done little to change that calculation.

The market may have found a reason to stop selling, but it hasn’t yet been given a particularly compelling reason to start chasing.

That is why the next couple of sessions matter, although I wouldn’t place too much emphasis on Friday’s shortened US trading day. Holiday liquidity can exaggerate moves in either direction, and with many senior traders likely extending their Thanksgiving break, the more meaningful test may not arrive until Monday.

That’s when the larger risk books return to something resembling normal participation, and portfolio managers must decide whether Wednesday’s apparent double bottom justifies rebuilding exposure.

The Turkey Is on the Table. The Verdict Can Wait Until Monday.

For now, investors have something to be thankful for. Wednesday’s late-session buying rescued the Nasdaq 100 from a deeply uncomfortable position, and Thursday’s response across Europe and Asia suggests that the appetite for beaten-down technology shares hasn’t disappeared.

The recovery also has a reasonable fundamental argument. Corporate earnings haven’t suffered the deterioration implied by some of the recent price action, AI investment expectations remain strong, and valuations have become more appealing after November’s sharp correction.

But there is still a difference between recognizing an opportunity and declaring the correction finished.

With the Fed’s December decision approaching, market volatility remains elevated, and much of Wall Street is away for Thanksgiving; Thursday’s advance deserves respect without being mistaken for a definitive change in direction.

My sense is that investors are beginning to treat the apparent double bottom as an opportunity to rebuild some exposure, rather than automatically viewing every bounce as another chance to sell. That’s an encouraging change in behaviour, even if the evidence remains preliminary.

And perhaps that is all we need to take away from this Thanksgiving session. After weeks of violent reversals, the market has finally managed to string together a little optimism without immediately handing it all back. Asia and Europe have followed Wall Street’s lead, a few AI cheapies are returning to portfolios, and the immediate urge to liquidate appears to have faded.

Not a bad outcome after the week we’ve had.

But with the senior dealing desks largely empty, I’d rather wait until Monday before deciding whether the market has genuinely found its feet or simply enjoyed a rather pleasant Thanksgiving holiday.

data.title: EUR-USD: Peak Seasonality At Year-End
data.description:
Today I’m showing you one of my favorite seasonal patterns. It’s about the US dollar, and I’ll present it to you using the euro-dollar currency pair.

Why is it one of my favorite patterns? I prefer time windows of at least a week, preferably longer. As a quantitative trading system developer, I have not managed to program a stable system for the forex market in this time window.

There are exceptions, though, and seasonality provides them, especially the one at year-end.

So let’s take a look at the seasonal path of the euro against the US dollar.

The seasonal path of the euro-dollar pair in detail

The seasonal chart shows you the typical seasonal path of the euro against the US dollar. It was calculated from the average of returns over the past 26 years. The horizontal axis shows the point in the year, the vertical axis the level of the seasonal index. This way, you can see at a glance how the US dollar moves through the course of the year.

Euro against the US dollar, seasonal path, calculated over 26 years

Seasonally, the euro rises sharply ahead of the turn of the year. Source: Seasonax | View data

As you can see, the euro rises seasonally toward the end of the year. It is the strongest seasonal move of the year. After that, it weakens again. What do the results look like in detail?

Win rate: 73,1 percent

The bar chart shows you the return of the euro against the US dollar over the past 26 years in the period between November 23 and December 20. In blue you see the years in which there were gains, in red those in which losses occurred.

Euro against the US dollar, return in percent between November 23 and December 20, in individual years since 2000

Most of the time, it went up. Source: Seasonax | View data

In 19 of the 26 cases, the euro rose during this phase at the turn of the year, with most of the losing years falling between 2007 and 2016. The average return was 1.9 percent, the annualized return 20.2 percent. Given the low volatility of currencies, that is quite a lot, as the seasonal chart already suggested.

The euro has only existed since the turn of the millennium. Other currencies, however, have existed much longer. They, too, show a comparable strength against the dollar at the turn of the year, going back as far as the 1970s. What is the reason for that?

The reason for the US dollar’s year-end slump

The rise of currencies against the dollar corresponds to a decline of the US dollar against those currencies. Since the phenomenon also occurs with other currencies, it is a phenomenon of the US dollar itself.

The US dollar’s reversal at the turn of the year is already a hint as to the reason for this seasonal pattern: it should be connected to the calendar year-end. And what happens at year-end? The balance sheet date!

The decline of the US dollar toward year-end is rooted in American tax law. Many American companies save on taxes by reporting the lowest possible amounts on the balance sheet date at year-end. In that case, it can be worthwhile to transfer funds to the accounts of foreign subsidiaries.

The additional demand for foreign currencies that this creates does not go without consequences for the exchange rate. That is why the US dollar typically falls toward year-end, while the euro and other currencies rise.

After the turn of the year, the tide turns. Companies transfer much of the funds back again, and the US dollar typically rises, while the euro and other currencies fall.

data.title: It’s A Thanksgiving Chart Party
data.description:
Charts 1, 2, and 3: What Is This?

On Wednesday, we saw a 3% intraday round trip, a seven-point move on the VIX and the S&P 500, taking us back to flat. Not Jerome Powell was wondering what they should call this pattern. I think it should be called the… “We need to talk…”

And I call it a dream trade for Volume Weighted Average Price…

The 705 call passed VWAP at $1.31 around 11:55 am.

That was at about $13.00 two hours later.

Just saying…

It was a big move with very little participation ahead of a holiday. But it’s a reminder of what can happen when you’re patient, and the fish does bite right when you need it.

So… now we head into Friday with Goldman and other banks calling the recent runs we’ve seen “bear market action.” Well… that’s good, because we are sitting heavily in cash and looking for trading opportunities like this while our signals are negative.

Chart 4: Another Reason for the Fed to Ease?

Yesterday, I talked about the “race to cash” theme of the last week in the market.

But there’s more to it than just selling to sell and raise cash. There’s another problem: companies are absorbing cash faster than they can earn it. Next year, the capex from the big hyperscalers will surpass $1.1 trillion.

Source: JPMorgan

We know they’re well past their cash flow, which means they must borrow from banks, issue bonds that people will buy instead of stocks, and drain money from funds.

One last thing… they’re also less inclined to buy back stock.

This is all draining liquidity from the equity market…

It’s happening on a multi-month lag of up to six months.

These are the types of things that can fuel lower inflation and put the U.S. on a path back toward easing by the end of the first quarter. Recall, again, we need to refinance about $10.6 trillion at the Treasury level as well.

We still have a long way to go.

Chart 5: Forced Selling… More on Tap?

Nothing like a stock market that runs on rules, except when the rules force a level of selling in a week that surpasses the GDP of Zimbabwe.

On Wednesday, the Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) dropped 4.7%, hit bear market territory (down 20% from its peak), and then finished off just 0.6%. This sort of reversal has only happened 16 times since 1988… Again, no one can really explain all of this.

But, it feels like this became a “decline in selling” and not a big uptick in purchasing.

These types of things happen when we get to extremes where we start to experience a dramatic decline in fast-moving stocks.

There could… of course… be more selling. Goldman said trend and vol-control funds dumped $70 billion in stock… and that we could see another $100 billion this week.

Watch out for Friday. The good news is that if that selling does happen, we could finally reach a point where we can get some lower-volume bidding in early December, and into that Fed meeting. From there, I suppose we’ll just wait for the 2:35 trade.

Chart 6: When Gold Became a Risk Asset?

Gold prices aren’t trading like a haven…

Gold is trading like a risk asset.

It slumped about 9% from November 17 to 20, and then continued its downward pressure to under $3,500 yesterday. I called a local gold buyer (who appears to be overwhelmed by sellers) and he described the panic selling in the local physical market where I live as a “shit show.”

Gold has been moving with the semis, and more or less looks like an inverted dollar chart right now. Nothing is immune in a liquidation…

The one thing that I do want to note is that major desks keep talking about the 2018 cycle and will make the comparisons. But the metals are the major difference right now. Gold was up in 2018, while gold’s down 10.8% this year. The yen was strong then, and it’s week now. Copper is down 13%, more than double 2018’s decline.

So… let’s be clear here. Panic hit an extreme (and we’re in a place where a short-term bounce into the Fed meeting is plausible.) But keep in mind that a lot of funds are still protecting their gains from the year. While the capitulation from humans could be coming to a close, positioning over December will be difficult to project. Pensions will be buying stocks next week… we know this as we wrap up the month.

But is that really enough to get everyone excited to own things again?

Chart 7: Don’t Forget…

So… what comes next from the Federal Reserve?

Markets are pricing in a 25 basis point hike in December…

Source: CME Fed Watchk

We can see a 98% probability of a hike…

But there’s one thing that we should consider. Recall that Governor Waller has advocated for a 50 basis point hike… And he would be arguing for either 25 points in December and 25 in January… or 50 in December if there isn’t insight on what to expect in January.

That… by definition… makes this event a “Live Meeting.”

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh doesn’t like forward guidance, so he’s offered us none.

The desks in New York are speculating on what comes next. Several banks expect three interest rate hikes by March (I don’t really care about rate hikes when they’ll probably turn on whatever supportive policies they can in December or Q1 for the banking sector.)

That said, consumer confidence is running hot, GDP is 4.3%, and core inflation still ran hot. So, we’ll raise interest rates… at a time that growth is really driven by AI and tech spending…

Chart 8: The Thanksgiving tab.

You’ll sit down today for dinner… and probably wonder what the cost of it was…

Dinner for 10 people, according to one farm group’s annual farm survery, increased to $58.63, which was a 6.3% jump from 2025. What’s driving the hike?

Turkey costs 10% more ($23.68)…

Cranberry is up 8.8%, milk 8.6%, and dinner rolls about 7%.

One of the most important drivers in that? Diesel fuel, which is pushing $6.00 (or a 58% jump from last year).

Of course, companies like Aldi and Walmart are saying that they can do this dinner for much less… But it’s still a really good measurement of what stuff costs. Like the Chapwood Index, this survey is tracking what people really buy…

And not… the government offset numbers in tech that mask the real cost of living.

And Finally…

I want to wish everyone a very Happy Thanksgiving…

Every day it’s a joy to get up and cover the market live with everyone at Money Printer Pro… And we’ll be back tomorrow live at 8:30. So, I hope to that you enjoy the day. I wrote an article over at Eagle that reflected on wealth, and I’ll share it with you this weekend… They are publishing it first, but I want to make sure that you get a chance to see it this weekend… What real wealth is… and how to properly cherish it.

I’ll see everyone tomorrow. Happy Thanksgiving…

Goat Funded enters the rapidly growing perpetual futures market with the launch of its fourth trading brand.

Goat Funded today announced the launch of Goat Funded Perps, a perpetuals prop firm powered by Hyperliquid, offering traders access to simulated funded accounts through a structured risk management framework.

The launch comes amid growing demand for perpetual futures, which have become a dominant force in cryptocurrency derivatives trading. According to BitMEX, perpetual futures account for over 90% of crypto contract trading.

The rise of decentralised exchanges and on-chain trading infrastructure has further accelerated adoption, with platforms such as Hyperliquid playing an increasingly important role in the evolution of crypto derivatives markets.

Perpetual futures, commonly known as perps, are derivative contracts that track the price of an underlying asset without an expiration date. Their popularity among crypto traders has grown due to their flexibility, liquidity and continuous market access.

Unlike traditional financial markets with fixed trading hours, perpetuals markets operate 24 hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days a year. Goat Funded Perps brings the simulated funded trading model to this growing market, offering around-the-clock trading and same-day reward processing.

The platform is powered by Hyperliquid, a blockchain designed for high-performance decentralised trading. Its order book, matching engine and liquidation processes operate on-chain, providing transparency into how trades are executed.

data.title: Expect A Fiscal Year 2027 Initial Freeze In Military Spending
data.description:
Zero of Twelve Fiscal Year 2027 Funding Bills Have Passed Congress. Democrats take control January 3.

Fiscal Year 2027 Deadline Is December 11. Zero Chance.

Congress still haven’t enacted a single one of the 12 regular appropriations bills for FY2027.

The government is currently running on a continuing resolution (P.L. 119-103) that expires at 11:59 p.m. Eastern on December 11.

What to Expect

A full-year set of bills before the deadline is not happening. But this is the pattern, not the exception.

Since FY1977, Congress has needed at least one continuing resolution in all but three years.

Expect another continuing resolution, probably a short one that kicks the can into the next Congress.

How Often Are Zero of Twelve Spending Bills This Late?

In 21 of the 49 fiscal years since FY1977, Congress enacted zero regular appropriations bills by October 1.

Of those 21, 16 occurred after FY1997 (the last year all bills were finished on time).

In recent decades, starting the year with zero bills enacted has been the norm, not the exception. Since roughly 2011–2012, it has happened in most years.

What’s Different This Time?

In the 2026 midterms (November 3), Democrats won control of both the House and the Senate:

  • House: Democrats ended up with roughly 259 seats (their largest majority since 1992), Republicans ~173.

  • Senate: Democrats 56 (including 2 independents who caucus with them), Republicans 44. They flipped 9 seats.

Republicans currently hold both chambers in the lame-duck 119th Congress.

On January 3, 2027, that fully reverses when the 120th Congress convenes. The presidency remains with Trump, so it becomes divided government, but with Democrats holding the legislative branch.

Why this Changes the FY2027 Funding Dynamics

The underlying procedural failure (zero of 12 regular bills enacted this late) is not unusual.

What is different is the incentive structure created by the total switch:

  • Democrats have little reason to cut a full-year deal now. Waiting until January gives them control of both appropriations committees and much more leverage over spending levels, policy riders, and restrictions.

  • Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray and others have publicly preferred a short-term CR that pushes the real negotiations into the new Congress.

  • Republicans are trying to lock in as much as they can (especially on defense) while they still have the majority, but they need Democratic votes in the Senate to do almost anything.

  • Result: Stronger-than-usual pressure for another short CR rather than finishing any full-year bills before December 11.

How this Compares to Other Years

Lame-duck sessions after midterms often have some of these dynamics when control is about to change, but a full flip of both chambers at once is less common.

The fact that Democrats are about to take full control of Congress in January makes it less likely than usual that the current Republican majorities will finish any of the FY2027 bills on their own terms before the deadline.

Military Spending

Most reporting and lawmakers treat a full-year Defense appropriations bill (or any of the other 11) as very unlikely in the lame duck.

The expected outcome is another short-term CR, possibly running into early 2027.

The White House has already requested various defense “anomalies” (exceptions) for the next CR, including money for Trump’s Golden Dome idea, Trump-class battleships, and other programs.

The separate $350 billion reconciliation package the administration wanted for extra defense spending is widely described as dead or close to it.

Chris Coons (the top Democrat on Senate Defense Appropriations) said the final number will be closer to $1 trillion and will almost certainly be settled next year under the new Democratic majorities.

What Hegseth and the White House Requested

About $1.5 trillion total for FY2027 national defense:

  • Roughly $1.15 trillion in the regular (discretionary) base budget

  • Plus $350 billion through a separate reconciliation bill

This was framed as a roughly 42–44% increase over prior-year levels. It was the largest single-year defense request in modern history.

What Congress Has Moved

  • House Appropriations Committee Defense bill: ~$1.072 trillion

  • Senate Republicans’ Draft: ~$1.1 trillion

  • NDAA versions: roughly $1.14–1.15 trillion (authorization only – not funding)

The $350 billion reconciliation package is widely described as dead or extremely unlikely in the lame-duck session.

What’s Likely

Hegseth and the White House asked for $1.5 trillion. The near-term reality is another continuing resolution that largely freezes funding near existing levels.

Any final full-year number will almost certainly be set in 2027 after Democrats take control of both chambers, and it is unlikely to reach the full $1.5 trillion request.

Understanding “Initial“

My headline says “Expect a Fiscal Year 2027 Initial Freeze in Military Spending”

Unfortunately, budget compromises nearly always are more of this for more of that.

Republicans want more military spending and offer more social spending to get it. History says expect more of the same.

However, the combination 56 Democrat Senators and 259-260 Democrat House seats changes the dynamics a bit.

Note that Republicans failed to pass much legislation in the past two because a small minority of Republicans could block legislation.

The next Congress will be vastly different. Senate and House leaders cannot be held hostage by a few votes.

However, Trump has a veto. To get things Democrats want, they will need to either compromise or wait until 2028.

That compromise dynamic is not yet clear. But Democrats can force the issue on many bills. Trump will own the political consequences if he vetoes popular measures.

Either way, items such as Golden Dome and the proposed Trump-class warships look more likely to land on the ash heap of unfunded ideas.

Otherwise it’s wait-and-see, but the balance of leverage has clearly shifted.

data.title: Money Matters
data.description:
Among the world’s most important central banks, inflation is currently the main concern. Even in those parts of the world where the economy is weak, monetary policy is being driven primarily by the view that inflation is too high. This likely will change during the first half of next year, when the combination of lower inflation rates and slower economic growth rates causes economic weakness to become the overriding concern and prompts a major shift towards monetary easing. For at least another two months, however, it’s likely that central banks will be tightening the proverbial monetary screws and the ‘liquidity’ backdrop will remain problematic for most assets. One important aspect of the liquidity backdrop is the monetary inflation rate, as illustrated for some countries/regions by the monthly charts displayed below.

The latest data from the Fed indicate a year-over-year True Money Supply (TMS) growth rate (monetary inflation rate) of around 7% for the US. This means that US monetary inflation has returned to near its long-term average after the massive swings of 2020-2023. With the Fed focused on the inflation bounce of the past few months — an inflation bounce caused mainly by war-related supply issues — and with the US housing market in the doldrums, the US monetary inflation rate probably will fall over the next few months. However, by the second quarter of next year, the US monetary trend probably will turn upward as the Fed reacts to the declining price inflation and economic weakness that suddenly have appeared in its rearview mirror.

The following chart combines the US and euro-zone money supplies to create what we refer to as the G2 monetary inflation rate. The vertical red lines on this chart mark the starting times of the last three US recessions.

Like the Fed, the ECB is in monetary tightening mode in an effort to combat increases in prices caused mainly by supply issues. Therefore, the G2 monetary inflation rate probably will fall over the next few months.

Economically and monetarily, Australia and Canada are in similar situations. In both cases, the central bank is in monetary tightening mode because cost-of-living measures supposedly have risen too fast. Also, the residential housing market is weakening in both countries, which should result in less mortgage-related money creation by commercial banks.

In Australia’s case, new tax regulations that recently caused mortgage-related lending by commercial banks to drop sharply are weighing on the housing market and the monetary inflation rate. In Canada’s case, the housing market has been sluggish for years and is showing no signs of improvement.

With reference to the following charts, it’s reasonable to expect that the monetary inflation downward trends that began 9-12 months ago will continue over the next 6 months, adding downward pressure to house prices and helping to generate enough economic weakness to set the stage for central bank policy reversals by the middle of 2027.

The People’s Bank of China (PBOC) is the only major central bank that currently is not leaning in the direction of monetary tightening. However, it also isn’t inflating aggressively. As illustrated below, China’s M1 money-supply growth rate has been making lower highs and lower lows since the start of 2010.

The direction of the next significant move in China’s monetary inflation rate will be important for gold and commodities, as it tends to influence prices in these markets with a variable lag. For example, a rise in China’s M1 growth rate to above the late-2025 high would eventually be supportive for the prices of gold and many other metals.
